expectedText:
FAMILY CODE SECTION 271 SANCTIONS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Pat Morgan

ABOUT THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet explains California Family Code section 271, a fee-shifting sanctions provision that a family court may apply in the proceeding between Jordan Lee and Pat Morgan, case number CGC-26-123456, filed in Sacramento County. It states the text of the statute and how published California Court of Appeal decisions have described and applied it. It does not tell either party whether a section 271 sanction should be requested, opposed, or is likely to be granted in this or any other case, and it is not a substitute for advice from a licensed attorney about the facts of a specific matter.

THE SECTION 271 STANDARD: CONDUCT THAT FURTHERS OR FRUSTRATES SETTLEMENT POLICY
Family Code section 271(a) states that, notwithstanding any other provision of the Family Code, a court may base an award of attorney's fees and costs on the extent to which the conduct of each party or attorney furthers or frustrates the policy of the law to promote settlement of litigation and, where possible, to reduce the cost of litigation by encouraging cooperation between the parties and attorneys. The statute states that an award under this section is in the nature of a sanction. The statute further states that in making an award under this section, the court must take into consideration all evidence concerning the parties' incomes, assets, and liabilities, and that the court may not impose a sanction under this section that imposes an unreasonable financial burden on the party against whom the sanction is imposed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) Notwithstanding any other provision of this code, the court may base an award of attorney’s fees and costs on the extent to which any conduct of each party or attorney furthers or frustrates the policy of the law to promote settlement of litigation and, where possible, to reduce the cost of litigation by encouraging cooperation between the parties and attorneys. An award of attorney’s fees and costs pursuant to this section is in the nature of a sanction. In making an award pursuant to this section, the court shall take into consideration all evidence concerning the parties’ incomes, assets, and liabilities. The court shall not impose a sanction pursuant to this section that imposes an unreasonable financial burden on the party against whom the sanction is imposed."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 271(a) (California Legislative Information text), the standard for a section 271 sanction, its nature as a sanction, and the income/assets/liabilities and unreasonable-financial-burden limits on it (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=271.)
  Known gap: This clause covers Family Code section 271(a) except its final sentence, which states that the requesting party need not show financial need and is addressed in a separate clause. It does not cover subdivision (b) (notice and an opportunity to be heard) or subdivision (c) (the source from which the award is payable), each addressed in a separate clause. The statute does not define 'unreasonable financial burden' numerically or otherwise, and does not state how a court is to weigh a party's income, assets, and liabilities against a proposed sanction amount on any particular record.

NO SHOWING OF FINANCIAL NEED REQUIRED
Family Code section 271(a) states that, in order to obtain an award under this section, the party requesting an award of attorney's fees and costs is not required to demonstrate any financial need for the award. Published California Court of Appeal decisions have described section 271 in the same terms: one decision stated that section 271 authorizes sanctions to advance the policy of promoting settlement of litigation and encouraging cooperation of the litigants, and does not require any actual injury, and that a party seeking a section 271 sanction is not required to establish any particular harm as a prerequisite to the award. That same decision stated that because section 271 is not a need-based statute and does not require a correlation between the sanctioned conduct and specific attorney's fees, the requesting party need not demonstrate her own current financial situation, and that a section 271 sanction need not be limited to the cost the sanctioned conduct actually imposed on the other side.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "In order to obtain an award under this section, the party requesting an award of attorney’s fees and costs is not required to demonstrate any financial need for the award."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 271(a) (California Legislative Information text), the statute's own statement that no financial need must be shown to obtain a section 271 award (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=271.)
  "“Section 271, subdivision (a) authorizes sanctions to advance the policy of promoting settlement of litigation and encouraging cooperation of the litigants” and “does not require any actual injury.”"
  — In re Marriage of Corona (2009) 172 Cal.App.4th 1205, 1225 [92 Cal.Rptr.3d 17], quoting In re Marriage of Feldman (2007) 153 Cal.App.4th 1470, 1479-1480, section 271 advances settlement/cooperation policy and does not require any actual injury (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2287840/in-re-marriage-of-corona/)
  "Claire was not required to establish any particular harm as a prerequisite to a sanctions award under section 271."
  — In re Marriage of Corona (2009) 172 Cal.App.4th 1205, 1226 [92 Cal.Rptr.3d 17], citing In re Marriage of Feldman (2007) 153 Cal.App.4th 1470, 1479-1480, no particular harm need be established as a prerequisite to a section 271 award (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2287840/in-re-marriage-of-corona/)
  "Because section 271 is not a need-based statute and does not require a correlation between the sanctioned conduct and specific attorney fees"
  — In re Marriage of Corona (2009) 172 Cal.App.4th 1205, 1226 [92 Cal.Rptr.3d 17], section 271 is not a need-based statute and does not require correlating the conduct to specific fees (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2287840/in-re-marriage-of-corona/)
  "a sanctions award under section 271 need not “be limited to the cost to the other side resulting from the bad conduct.”"
  — In re Marriage of Corona (2009) 172 Cal.App.4th 1205, 1226 [92 Cal.Rptr.3d 17], quoting In re Marriage of Quay (1993) 18 Cal.App.4th 961, 970, a section 271 award need not be limited to the other side's actual cost from the bad conduct (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2287840/in-re-marriage-of-corona/)
  Known gap: The 'does not require any actual injury' language quoted here comes from In re Marriage of Corona, which was itself quoting and applying In re Marriage of Feldman; this clause does not independently trace or re-verify every authority that Corona or Feldman in turn rely on for these propositions. This clause states how these two published decisions described section 271's no-need, no-actual-injury character; it does not survey the full body of section 271 case law for contrary or qualifying statements, and it does not address Family Code section 2030's separate need-based standard, which is covered in a different document in this corpus.

NOTICE AND AN OPPORTUNITY TO BE HEARD; SOURCE OF PAYMENT
Family Code section 271(b) states that an award of attorney's fees and costs as a sanction under this section may be imposed only after notice by the requesting party or the court to the party against whom the sanction is proposed, and an opportunity for that party to be heard. Family Code section 271(c) states that such an award is payable only from the property or income of the party against whom the sanction is imposed, except that the award may be made against the sanctioned party's share of the community property.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(b) An award of attorney’s fees and costs as a sanction pursuant to this section shall be imposed only after notice by the requesting party or the court to the party against whom the sanction is proposed and opportunity for that party to be heard is provided by the court."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 271(b) (California Legislative Information text), the notice-and-opportunity-to-be-heard requirement before a section 271 sanction may be imposed (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=271.)
  "(c) An award of attorney’s fees and costs as a sanction pursuant to this section is payable only from the property or income of the party against whom the sanction is imposed, except that the award may be against the sanctioned party’s share of the community property."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 271(c) (California Legislative Information text), the source from which a section 271 award is payable (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=271.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes subdivisions (b) and (c) of Family Code section 271 in full; it does not address what specific form of notice (for example, a noticed motion or order to show cause versus another mechanism) satisfies subdivision (b) on particular facts, or how a court identifies a party's 'share of the community property' under subdivision (c) before a final division of community property has occurred. Those questions are not resolved by the statutory text alone.

CASE LAW: STANDARD OF REVIEW AND APPLICATION WITHOUT AN INDEPENDENT BAD-FAITH FINDING
A section 271 sanctions order is reviewed on appeal for abuse of discretion. Applying that standard, California courts have stated that the trial court's order will be overturned only if, considering all the evidence viewed most favorably in support of the order, no judge could reasonably make the order. In one published decision applying this standard, the Court of Appeal affirmed a section 271 sanctions award as an alternative basis for a sanction the family court had also described using the language of Code of Civil Procedure sanctions provisions, including a finding that a party's conduct was in "bad faith"; the appellate court's section 271 analysis did not treat a separate bad-faith finding as a required element, instead relying on the statute's furthers-or-frustrates-settlement-policy standard and on the absence of any requirement that the requesting party show particular harm.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“A sanction order under . . . section 271 is reviewed under the abuse of discretion standard. ‘ “[T]he trial court’s order will be overturned only if, considering all the evidence viewed most favorably in support of its order, no judge could reasonably make the order.” ’ ”"
  — In re Marriage of Feldman (2007) 153 Cal.App.4th 1470, 1478 [64 Cal.Rptr.3d 29], quoting In re Marriage of Burgard (1999) 72 Cal.App.4th 74, 82, abuse-of-discretion standard of review for a section 271 sanctions order (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2284647/in-re-marriage-of-feldman/)
  "Claire was not required to establish any particular harm as a prerequisite to a sanctions award under section 271."
  — In re Marriage of Corona (2009) 172 Cal.App.4th 1205, 1226 [92 Cal.Rptr.3d 17], citing In re Marriage of Feldman (2007) 153 Cal.App.4th 1470, 1479-1480, no particular harm need be established as a prerequisite to a section 271 award, applied where the family court had also invoked bad-faith language under a different statute (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2287840/in-re-marriage-of-corona/)
  Known gap: This clause describes how one published Court of Appeal decision (In re Marriage of Corona) applied section 271 to conduct that the family court had also labeled 'bad faith' under a different, non-family-law sanctions statute; it does not establish that a 'bad faith' finding is legally irrelevant to every section 271 case, and it is not a survey of the full body of section 271 case law on that question — only the decisions actually reviewed for this document are described here. It also does not describe the underlying facts of the cited decision (a dispute over housing-cost arrearages) as establishing what conduct will or will not qualify for a sanction in a different case.

HOW SECTION 271 DIFFERS FROM SECTION 2030 AND THE DISCLOSURE SANCTIONS STATUTES
Family Code section 271 is codified in Part 5 (Attorney's Fees and Costs) of Division 2 (General Provisions) of the Family Code, and by its own terms applies notwithstanding any other provision of the code. California case law has described a section 271 analysis as one that does not consider the relative circumstances of the respective parties, but instead focuses on the behavior of an individual party or attorney — in contrast with a need-based fee award under Family Code section 2030, which turns on the parties' relative circumstances. Unlike cost shifting under section 2030, a section 271 award is described in the statute itself as in the nature of a sanction, subject to the statute's own limits that it may not impose an unreasonable financial burden on the sanctioned party and is payable only from that party's property or income (or the party's share of community property). Family Code sections 2100-2113, covered in a separate document in this corpus, authorize a different, mandatory sanctions and judgment-set-aside remedy limited to a party's noncompliance with the disclosure chapter's specific financial-disclosure requirements; section 271 is not limited to disclosure violations and, by its statutory standard, may be based on any conduct of a party or attorney that furthers or frustrates the policy of promoting settlement and reducing litigation costs through cooperation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The section 271 analysis does not consider the relative circumstances of the respective parties, but focuses on the behavior of an individual party and his or her counsel. Section 271 allows the trial court to reward or punish conduct by a party or attorney that “furthers or frustrates the policy of the law to promote settlement of litigation and, where possible, to reduce the cost of litigation by encouraging cooperation between the parties and attorneys.” (§ 271, subd. (a).) Unlike cost shifting under section 2030, a section 271 award is “in the nature of a sanction.” (§ 271, subd. (a).)"
  — In re Marriage of Smith (2015) 242 Cal.App.4th 529, 536, fn. 6 [195 Cal.Rptr.3d 162], section 271 focuses on individual conduct rather than relative circumstances, and is described as a sanction (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/3156704/marriage-of-smith/)
  "Nevertheless, the trial court may not impose a sanction under section 271 that “imposes an unreasonable financial burden on the party against whom the sanction is imposed.” (Id., subd. (a).) Section 271 provides that an award under that section “is payable only from the property or income of the party against whom the sanction is imposed, except that the award may be against the sanctioned party’s share of the community property.” (Id., subd. (c).)"
  — In re Marriage of Smith (2015) 242 Cal.App.4th 529, 536, fn. 6 [195 Cal.Rptr.3d 162], the unreasonable-financial-burden limit and community-property source of payment restated (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/3156704/marriage-of-smith/)
  "PART 5. ATTORNEY'S FEES AND COSTS [270 - 274]"
  — Cal. Fam. Code, Div. 2, Pt. 5 heading (California Legislative Information text), section 271's placement within the Attorney's Fees and Costs part of the code's general provisions, distinct from the disclosure chapter containing sections 2100-2113 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=271.)
  Known gap: The case-law portion of this clause quotes a single Court of Appeal footnote comparing section 271 to section 2030 specifically; that footnote did not address the disclosure sanctions statutes, Family Code sections 2100-2113. The statement that section 271 is not limited to disclosure violations reflects this document's own reading of section 271's general, code-wide 'notwithstanding any other provision of this code' text and its placement in a different part of the code from the disclosure chapter, rather than a case holding addressing that specific three-way comparison. This clause does not resolve whether particular conduct could support relief under more than one of these three provisions at once, or how a court would sequence or combine such requests.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Jordan Lee and Pat Morgan acknowledge having reviewed this information sheet describing Family Code section 271, including its standard for sanctions based on conduct that furthers or frustrates the policy of promoting settlement and cooperation, its statement that no financial need must be shown, its income/assets/liabilities and unreasonable-financial-burden limits, its notice requirement, and how it differs from Family Code section 2030 and the disclosure sanctions statutes at Family Code sections 2100-2113. Signed in Oakland, California on September 1, 2026.
